extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, journalists, and informed readers interested in public opinion and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria for understanding how public opinion is formed, segmented, propagated, and how it acts (legal and extra-legal channels) in Britain and the United States; useful to researchers, communicators, and reformers planning to influence mass opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three orders of men in the South
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three orders of men in the South: (1) the upper or educated class (children of the planting aristocracy and Northern settlers in towns) who largely belong to the Democratic party; (2) the 'Mean Whites' — a poor, shiftless, often ignorant rural class formerly economically superfluous under slavery; (3) the negroes, who constitute about one-third of the population in the old Slave States and dominate Southern politics by their presence though they 'cannot be said to form or influence opinion'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite social classification when analysing local Southern opinion: note the political alignment, capacities for independent judgment, economic bases, and how each group's interests and status shape their political behaviour. Example implications: the upper class provides leadership and coherent policy views; the mean whites have been followers but are becoming independent actors; the negro population's political exclusion (and attempts to prevent their voting) has major influence on events even if they do not form dominant opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uneven political knowledge and capacity across the population
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Remembering that of the whole population of the Union, nearly one-third is in the Southern States, and that the majority of that one-third ... has no political knowledge or capacity, nothing that can be called rational opinion' — and that there is a large mass of recently arrived and ignorant immigrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree of 'political knowledge or capacity' in target populations before expecting deliberative engagement. Where large groups lack civic education, expect less reasoned opinion and greater susceptibility to simple appeals or party mobilization. This affects the realism of appeals to 'enlightened democracy' and the design of communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional change and homogenization of opinion over time
rubrics_metrics.description: As the West (including Pacific States) grows it loses some distinctive features and becomes more like the East; centres of literary and intellectual activity scatter; opinion will be more homogeneous and less local in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning long-term communication or policy campaigns, factor in that regional political characters evolve: tactics effective today in a particular region may lose potency as populations grow, migrate, and link culturally/financially to other regions. Anticipate homogenization of opinion and design scalable messages accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sets of persons who constitute British public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: In Britain public opinion may be distinguished into three sets: (1) those who make opinion — practical politicians, journalists, and a small fringe of professionals who think and talk constantly about public affairs (the 'working staff' of the laboratory); (2) those who receive and hold opinion — persons who watch public affairs, attend meetings, belong to associations and vote of their own accord; (3) those who have no opinions at all — the rest of the voters who do not care much about politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences into creators, engaged intermediates, and passive voters when diagnosing how views form and spread. The first set generates ideas; the second tests and adopts or rejects them; the third is mobilized chiefly at elections. Tailor messages and channels: intensive argumentation and press for the first set; persuasive, confidence-building messaging for the second; mobilization tactics (turnout, simple cues) for the third.

rubrics_metrics.name: The measure of the worth of a view: breadth of support and zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The measure of the worth of a view or proposal ... is not merely the breadth of the support it obtains, but also the zeal which it inspires in those who adopt it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals and campaigns both by how many endorse them and by the fervour those endorsers show. Mobilizing a smaller but zealous constituency can be more politically effective than a larger but lukewarm one. Use metrics that capture intensity (volunteerism, donations, turnout boosts) in addition to raw reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity is easy to obtain; struggle for public attention is severe
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Publicity is the easiest thing in the world to obtain; but as it is attainable by all notions, phrases, and projects, wise and foolish alike, the struggle for [public] attention is severe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting communications (e.g., press releases), assume noise and novelty competition: attention can be won quickly but is not a reliable indicator of quality. Prioritize distinctiveness, sustained framing, and repeat exposure rather than a single publicity spike. Beware anti-patterns: sensational but unsubstantive messages that attract attention but do not build durable support.

rubrics_metrics.name: In America, opinion 'grows' rather than being 'made' by a few
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike Britain where a relatively small organized set makes opinion, in America opinion 'does not originate in a particular class, but grows up in the nation at large' — many minds of similar knowledge and beliefs often arrive independently at the same idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect grassroots diffusion, spontaneous concurrence, and decentralized genesis of ideas in the U.S. Strategies that rely on seeding ideas widely (rather than imposing them from elite centres) and facilitating their organic spread (local chapters, press syndication) are often more effective. Examples cited: civil service reform, secret ballot, primaries, international copyright — all began with relatively few but spread by leavening public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for propagating a doctrine or movement
rubrics_metrics.description: When propagating a doctrine the methods used include forming a central society, establishing branch societies across the country, starting a journal (or journals), and holding annual conventions with speeches and resolutions. If a striking personality is connected with the movement he may serve as a figure-head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical movement-building structures: central organization + local branches + dedicated media + periodic national gatherings. Practical guidance: invest in sustained organizational capacity, media (journals/press), and leadership visibility. Anti-pattern: expecting a single speech or event to substitute for persistent organizational work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal machinery for influencing affairs is limited; unorganized opinion is helpless
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections are the primary constitutional channel; voting for a man is an inadequate way of expressing detailed policy because candidates differ from many supporters and party discipline limits individual legislators. 'A body of unorganized opinion is ... helpless ... obliged to organize.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of formal democratic mechanisms for translating diffuse opinion into policy. To influence legislation or executive action, organize (capture party platforms, create electoral incentives, build focused pressure groups). Tactical options include persuading a major party to adopt a view (most effective but difficult), or building separate organizational pressure outside normal party channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative influence of speeches, newspapers, and events in America
rubrics_metrics.description: In America speeches seem to influence the average citizen less (he does his own thinking), newspaper invective influences less because he is used to it, while current events influence more because he is better informed of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating to American audiences, prefer grounding messages in current, tangible events and facts rather than relying chiefly on rhetorical speeches or invective. Use event-driven stories, reporting, and data to sway the public; speeches can inform but are less likely to shift the average citizen unless tied to salient events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional vs amateur opinion-makers and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In England the profession of opinion-making is largely the work of specialists; in America most opinion-makers (except some journalists and statesmen) are amateurs who are primarily occupied with other avocations. This yields pros and cons: amateurs' books may have merits lacking in professionals', but American output is 'less coherent, less abundant, and less promptly effective' than the English product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether your communicators are specialists or amateurs. Specialist (professional) opinion-makers tend to produce coherent, abundant, and promptly effective messaging; amateurs can offer originality and authenticity but may lack coherence and reach. Strategy: where coherence and rapid impact are needed, partner with professional communicators or develop professional communication capacity.
